diagnosis.what_is_wrong: No kernel-level fault is established, so the reported longer coding task cannot be confirmed as caused by host or container contention. The trace shows a workload shift—CPU activity in the container drops around 03:27:35 and python3 begins sustained CPU execution around 03:27:41.5—but the observed disk, network, and scheduler samples do not identify a cause for abnormal delay.
diagnosis.evidence: Compared whole-trace ctf_timespan (03:27:30.200–03:28:02.100) and ctf_proclife; the synchronized process exits near 03:27:57.6–57.7 could be task/trace teardown, not demonstrated service failure. Whole-span timeline/aggregation showed an opening scheduler burst, but unrelated event series did not share a synchronized collapse. run_python showed container sched_stat_runtime falling from 245.7 CPU ms/s in 03:27:30–03:27:35 to 56.6 ms/s in 03:27:35–03:27:41, then recovering; python3 subsequently used about 3.17 CPU-seconds through 03:27:57, typically 24–25 ms per 100 ms. ctf_lines showed a sampled claude wake-to-switch interval of 17 µs and block completions under 1 ms; sampled network transmissions succeeded. Wake-to-run matching was incomplete and its long-tail estimates inconsistent across short intervals, so it does not establish contention. These checks would be falsified by sustained high wake-to-run delays or elevated I/O latency in the coding interval; the sampled evidence does not show that, but is not broad enough to rule out every intermittent delay.
diagnosis.window_evidence: The candidate CPU-activity trough is bounded by the measured decrease around 03:27:35 and recovery by about 03:27:45, while python3 starts around 03:27:41.5. Those are workload transitions, not verified fault boundaries: the trace provides no decisive mechanism or causal link to the reported task delay, and ends at 03:28:02.100. Therefore no incident window is supported.
